title: Magnet poles: why two magnets attract or repel

summary.text: Hold two magnets end to end. One way round, they snap together. Turn one round, and they push each other apart. Every magnet has two ends where its force is strongest, called poles: a north pole and a south pole. A north pole and a south pole attract each other. Two north poles, or two south poles, repel each other. Iron that is not a magnet is attracted by both poles, so only a magnet can repel a magnet. Cut a magnet in two, and each piece has its own north and south pole. Nobody has ever found a north pole on its own. In this unit you float two magnets on water and find out what a free magnet does when it is pushed away.
summary.art: Two bar magnets on a table, red north ends and blue south ends. One pair snaps together north to south. The other pair, north facing north, has a small gap and arrows pushing apart.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold one bar magnet in each hand. Bring their ends slowly together. Now turn one magnet round and try again. One way, they jump together. The other way, you feel a push, though nothing is touching. Why does the same magnet do two different things?
intro.text: The answer is in the two ends of every magnet, its poles. In this unit you find which end is north and which is south, and you learn the rule for when magnets attract and when they repel. Then you float two magnets on water, push one away, and watch what it does next. A French scholar called Petrus Peregrinus did the same test with magnet stones in 1269.
intro.art: A child's two hands holding two bar magnets with a small gap between them, and small curved arrows showing a push between the ends.

outcomes: I can say that every magnet has a north pole and a south pole, and find which end is which by letting the magnet turn freely.
I can use the rule: unlike poles attract, like poles repel.
I can explain why repelling is the sure test of a magnet, because plain iron is attracted by both poles.
I can run a fair test with two floating magnets, record what happens, and explain what a magnet that is free to turn does.
I can explain that cutting a magnet gives two magnets, each with a north and a south pole.
I can explain why the Earth's magnetic pole in the far north is really a south pole.
I can find the many poles hidden in a bendy fridge magnet.

terms.meaning: One of the two places on a magnet where its force is strongest. On a bar magnet, the poles are at the two ends.
terms.example: Roll a bar magnet in paper clips. Most clips cling to the two ends, the poles, and very few to the middle.
terms.art: A bar magnet with bunches of paper clips at both ends and a bare middle.

terms.meaning: The end of a magnet that turns to point north when the magnet can swing freely. Its full name is the north-seeking pole.
terms.example: Float a bar magnet on a plastic lid in a tub of water. When it stops turning, the end pointing north is its north pole.
terms.art: A bar magnet on a floating lid, its red end pointing to a letter N.

terms.meaning: The end of a magnet that turns to point south when the magnet can swing freely.
terms.example: The floating bar magnet's other end points south. That end is its south pole.
terms.art: A bar magnet on a floating lid, its blue end pointing to a letter S.

terms.meaning: To draw something closer. Two magnets attract when a north pole faces a south pole.
terms.example: Bring the north pole of one magnet near the south pole of another. They jump together and stick.
terms.art: Two bar magnets snapping together, red end to blue end, with arrows pointing towards each other.

terms.meaning: To push something away without touching it. Two magnets repel when two north poles, or two south poles, face each other.
terms.example: Push two north poles towards each other. You feel a push, and the magnet on the table slides away.
terms.art: Two bar magnets with red ends facing, a gap between, and arrows pointing apart.

terms.meaning: Poles of the same kind: two north poles, or two south poles. Like poles repel.
terms.example: Two south poles brought together push apart.
terms.art: Two blue ends facing each other with a gap, labelled S and S.

terms.meaning: Poles of different kinds: a north pole and a south pole. Unlike poles attract.
terms.example: A north pole and a south pole snap together.
terms.art: A red end and a blue end stuck together, labelled N and S.

terms.meaning: The push or pull between magnets, or between a magnet and iron. It acts across a gap, and gets weaker quickly as the gap grows.
terms.example: A floating magnet starts to move when another magnet comes within a few centimetres.
terms.art: A hand-held magnet a few centimetres from a magnet on a floating lid, with a ruler between them.

terms.meaning: The space around a magnet where its force acts. Scientists draw it as lines that come out of the north pole and go into the south pole.
terms.example: A compass needle near a bar magnet turns to follow the field lines.
terms.art: A bar magnet with curved lines looping from its north end round to its south end.

terms.meaning: A piece of iron or steel that acts as a magnet only while a magnet is near it or touching it.
terms.example: A paper clip hanging from a magnet can hold a second clip. Take the magnet away, and the second clip falls.
terms.art: A magnet with a chain of three paper clips hanging from it.

terms.meaning: A magnet shaped like a straight bar, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.
terms.example: School magnet sets usually have two bar magnets with red or N on the north end.
terms.art: Two painted bar magnets, half red and half blue, lying side by side.

explanations.definition: Every magnet has at least one north pole and one south pole. The poles are where its force is strongest.
explanations.description: On a bar magnet the poles are at the two ends, so paper clips cling there and hardly at all in the middle. A magnet that can turn freely, hanging on a thread or floating on water, always settles with one end pointing north. That end is called the north pole, and the other end is the south pole. Many school magnets are painted red at the north end, or marked N.
examples: A bar magnet floating on a plastic lid turns until it points north and south.
A round fridge magnet has its poles on its two flat faces, not on its edge.
explanations.art: A bar magnet with N and S labels, paper clips bunched at each end, and an arrow from N towards a compass rose.
explanations.context: This card explains what the poles of a magnet are, and how to tell north from south.

explanations.concept: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel
explanations.definition: A north pole and a south pole attract each other. Two north poles repel each other, and so do two south poles.
explanations.description: This is the rule for every magnet, big or small. The force works across a gap, so the magnets do not need to touch. The closer the poles are, the stronger the force. Move them a little further apart, and the force drops quickly. That is why a floating magnet sits still until the other magnet comes close, and then suddenly moves.
examples: The magnetic catch on a cupboard door holds because unlike poles, or a magnet and steel, attract.
A toy train with magnet links will not join if one carriage is turned round, because like poles face each other.
explanations.art: Three pairs of bar magnets: N facing S with arrows together, N facing N and S facing S with arrows apart.
explanations.context: This card gives the rule for when two magnets attract and when they repel.

explanations.concept: A magnet that is free to turn ends up attracting
explanations.definition: When like poles face each other and one magnet is free to turn, it swings round until its other pole faces the first magnet. Then the two attract.
explanations.description: Repelling pushes a magnet away, but it also twists it. Unless something holds the magnet straight, it turns round, so a north pole ends up facing a south pole. Then the two magnets come together. This is what you see when two magnets float on water. Scientists have shown that ordinary magnets on their own can never hold another magnet floating still in the air. Something else must hold it in place, like a pencil through ring magnets or a spinning top.
examples: Two floating magnets pushed north to north turn round and stick together.
Ring magnets on a pencil float one above another. Pull the pencil out, and the top ring flips over and sticks.
explanations.art: Two bar magnets on floating lids: first pushing apart, then one turning round, then stuck together north to south.
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the floating magnets experiment: why a pushed-away magnet does not stay away.

explanations.concept: Iron is attracted by both poles
explanations.definition: Iron and steel that are not magnets are attracted by the north pole and by the south pole. They are never repelled.
explanations.description: When a magnet comes near a steel paper clip, the clip becomes a temporary magnet. The end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted. That means attraction cannot tell you whether a thing is a magnet or plain iron. Only repelling can. If something pushes away one end of your magnet, it must be a magnet too.
examples: A steel spoon sticks to both ends of a bar magnet.
Two wrapped objects look the same. The one that pushes away one end of your magnet is the magnet.
explanations.art: A paper clip stuck to the N end and another stuck to the S end of a bar magnet, with small S and N letters on the clips' touching ends.
explanations.context: This card explains why repelling is the sure test of a magnet.

explanations.concept: Cut a magnet, and you get two magnets
explanations.definition: If you cut or break a magnet, each piece has its own north pole and south pole.
explanations.description: Inside a magnet, countless tiny magnets point the same way, each with its own north and south. The north pole of a magnet is just where the north ends of these tiny magnets come out at the surface. Cut the bar anywhere, and new poles appear at the cut, one north and one south. Even an electron, the tiniest magnet known, has a north and a south. Nobody has ever found a north pole on its own.
examples: Cut a bendy fridge magnet strip in half. Both halves still stick to the fridge.
Petrus Peregrinus broke a lodestone in 1269 and found that both pieces had a north and a south pole.
explanations.art: A bar magnet cut into two, then four, pieces, each piece with its own N and S labels and tiny arrows inside all pointing the same way.
explanations.context: This card explains why you can never get a north pole on its own by cutting a magnet.

explanations.concept: The Earth's far north is a magnetic south pole
explanations.definition: The Earth is a giant magnet. Its magnetic pole near the North Pole is a south pole, because it attracts the north poles of compass needles.
explanations.description: A magnet's north pole is named for the direction it points. Unlike poles attract, so the place it points to must be a south pole. Maps call that place the North Magnetic Pole, which can be confusing. It sits in the Arctic, not exactly at the North Pole, and it moves a little every year.
examples: A compass needle's north pole points north, towards the Earth's magnetic south pole.
Over hundreds of thousands of years, the Earth's magnetic poles have swapped places many times.
explanations.art: The Earth with a giant bar magnet drawn inside, its S end under the Arctic, and a small compass needle with its N end pointing up towards it.
explanations.context: This card explains a puzzle about the names of the poles.

explanations.concept: Bendy fridge magnets have many poles
explanations.definition: A bendy fridge magnet has thin stripes of north and south poles side by side on its magnetic face.
explanations.description: The stripes are a few millimetres wide. Press two bendy magnets face to face and slide one across the other. In one direction it slides smoothly. In the other, it bumps, because it crosses stripes that attract and repel in turn. Having many poles close together makes the magnet hold strongly to the fridge from very close, while its force dies away very close to its face. Its back face hardly attracts at all.
examples: Slide two fridge magnets face to face. Feel the bumps.
The back of a bendy fridge magnet does not stick to the fridge.
explanations.art: Close-up of a bendy fridge magnet's back, with thin stripes coloured red and blue in turn.
explanations.context: This card explains what you feel when you slide two bendy fridge magnets over each other.

explanations.concept: Could a north pole exist on its own?
explanations.description: Some physicists' theories say a single north pole, without a south pole, could exist. They call it a magnetic monopole. On 14 February 1982, a detector run by Blas Cabrera at Stanford University recorded one signal that looked like a monopole passing through. It never happened again. Many larger searches since have found none. So nobody knows yet whether monopoles exist.
examples: Every magnet ever tested has had both a north and a south pole.
Scientists still search for monopoles in rocks, in space and in giant machines.
explanations.art: A scientist in a 1980s laboratory watching a single spike on a long paper chart from a coil of wire.
explanations.context: This card is about an open question: can a north pole exist without a south pole?

agreed.text: Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Unlike poles attract, and like poles repel.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can check it with two magnets. Petrus Peregrinus wrote it down from his own tests in 1269.

agreed.text: Cutting a magnet gives two magnets, each with both poles.
agreed.evidence: It has been tested on magnets of every size, down to single atoms and electrons, which are themselves tiny magnets with two poles.

agreed.text: Plain iron and steel are attracted by both poles, never repelled.
agreed.evidence: Test a steel spoon on each end of a magnet. A magnet turns the nearby iron into a temporary magnet with the opposite pole facing it.

agreed.text: The Earth is a magnet, and its magnetic pole in the Arctic is a magnetic south pole.
agreed.evidence: The north poles of compass needles all over the world point towards it, and unlike poles attract.

agreed.text: Ordinary magnets on their own cannot hold another magnet floating still in the air.
agreed.evidence: Samuel Earnshaw proved this in 1842. Every magnet that seems to float is held by something else, such as a pencil, a spin or an electric current.

challenging.claim: If a thing sticks to a magnet, it must be a magnet.
challenging.against: A steel spoon sticks to a magnet too, and it is not a magnet. Only repelling proves that something is a magnet.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake when testing for magnets.

challenging.claim: You can cut a magnet so that one piece is all north and the other all south.
challenging.for: The north pole is at one end and the south pole at the other, so cutting in the middle seems to split them.
challenging.against: Every piece has both poles. New poles appear at the cut.
challenging.context: This card is about what happens when a magnet is cut.

challenging.claim: The north pole of a magnet is the stronger end.
challenging.for: Many sets paint the north end red, which looks more important.
challenging.against: Both poles of a bar magnet are equally strong. Test it: count the paper clips each end picks up.
challenging.context: This card is about whether one pole is stronger.

challenging.claim: The compass points to the Pole Star, or to iron mines in the far north.
challenging.who: Many people in the Middle Ages
challenging.for: The needle points north, where the Pole Star shines.
challenging.against: In 1269 Petrus Peregrinus argued against the iron mines, because magnet stones are found in many lands. Later, William Gilbert showed that the Earth itself is a magnet.
challenging.context: This card is about old ideas for why a compass points north.

challenging.claim: A wheel of magnets can turn forever and power a machine.
challenging.who: Many inventors, including Petrus Peregrinus in 1269
challenging.for: Magnets attract and repel without being pushed, so it seems they could keep a wheel turning.
challenging.against: Every such wheel stops. A magnet's force pulls a wheel forward in one place and holds it back in another, so it gives no free energy. Peregrinus also thought the iron teeth would be repelled, but iron is attracted by both poles.
challenging.context: This card is about the dream of a magnet motor that runs forever.

challenging.claim: Single magnetic poles, monopoles, exist somewhere in the universe.
challenging.who: Some physicists, from Paul Dirac in 1931 onwards
challenging.for: Some theories of physics predict them. One possible signal was seen in 1982.
challenging.against: No search since has found one, and that signal was never repeated.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a north pole can exist on its own.

big_questions.q: When you cut a magnet, a new north pole and a new south pole appear at the cut. Were they there before you cut it?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tiny magnets inside, each with its own north and south.

big_questions.q: Why does a pushed-away magnet turn round instead of staying away?
big_questions.hint: Watch the floating magnets again. Which part of the magnet is pushed, and which part is pulled?

big_questions.q: A magnet's north pole points to a place we call the North Magnetic Pole, which is really a magnetic south pole. Do names describe things, or only help us talk about them?
big_questions.hint: Who chose the names, and what did they know at the time?

big_questions.q: Could a north pole ever exist without a south pole?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have searched for one for nearly a hundred years. What would finding one change?

big_questions.q: Two magnets that repel each other are using the same force as two that attract. Are attracting and repelling two different things, or one thing seen two ways?
big_questions.hint: In the float test, what did the repelling magnet do next?

big_questions.q: You can feel a magnet push your hand, but you cannot see anything there. Is the magnetic field a real thing, or a way of describing what magnets do?
big_questions.hint: A compass needle placed anywhere near a magnet turns. What does that tell you about the space around it?

story.title: The Carriage That Would Not Join
story.note: Channapatna, a town between Bengaluru and Mysuru in Karnataka, really is famous for its bright lacquered wooden toys. Lakshmi, her grandparents and the toy train are made up.
text: In Channapatna, the town of wooden toys, Lakshmi's grandparents had a small workshop at the back of their house. The air smelled of fresh wood and warm lac, the coloured wax that makes the toys shine. Paati turned the wood on the lathe. Thatha painted it. Lakshmi was nine, and in the summer holidays she was allowed to help.

That summer, a shop in Bengaluru had ordered fifty toy trains. Each train had an engine and three carriages, painted red, yellow and green. Paati had a clever plan for joining them. At each end of every carriage, she set a small round magnet into the wood, flat side out. Then the carriages would click together when they touched, with no hooks to break.

On Monday, Thatha fitted the magnets. On Tuesday, he lined up the first train on the workbench. The engine clicked onto the red carriage. The red carriage clicked onto the yellow one. But when he pushed the green carriage towards the yellow one, it would not join. It slid away across the bench, as if the yellow carriage had pushed it.
Thatha frowned. He pushed it again. It slid away again. 'This magnet is broken,' he said. 'I will glue a hook on instead.'
Lakshmi watched the green carriage. When Thatha pushed it, it did not just slide. It also twisted a little, sideways, as if it wanted to turn round. 'Wait, Thatha,' she said. 'Don't glue it yet.'
She picked up the green carriage, turned it round, and brought its other end to the yellow carriage. Click. The two joined at once.
Thatha stared. 'So the magnet works after all. But why did it push away the first time?'

Lakshmi had learned this from Paati, who had read it in an old science book. 'Every magnet has two poles, a north pole and a south pole,' she said. 'A north pole and a south pole attract. Two north poles repel. So do two south poles. When you put the magnets in, Thatha, some went in with north facing out, and some with south facing out. The green carriage had its north facing the yellow carriage's north.'
'Then I must take every magnet out and test it,' said Thatha, looking at the forty-nine trains still waiting.

Lakshmi shook her head. 'No. We only need one rule. Every carriage must have north facing out at the front, and south facing out at the back. Then every front joins every back, whichever carriage you pick.'
'But how do I know which side of a round magnet is north?' asked Thatha. 'They all look the same.'

Lakshmi thought about it. Then she fetched a plastic tiffin lid and the big plastic tub that Paati used for soaking cloth. She filled the tub with water and floated the lid in the middle. On the lid she stood one of the round magnets on its edge, held up by a little lump of clay, so that its flat faces pointed sideways.

Slowly, the lid began to turn. After a minute it stopped. One flat face pointed towards the front door, and the other towards the back wall. Lakshmi checked Paati's old compass. 'This face points north,' she said, and put a dot of red paint on it. 'That is the north pole.'

'Now we have one magnet we know,' she said. 'For all the others, we do not need the tub. Hold each new magnet near the red dot. If it is pushed away, the face towards the dot is north too. If it is pulled in, it is south.'

Thatha tried it with a new magnet. It jumped and stuck to the red dot. 'South,' he said, and marked it blue. The next one pushed away from the red dot and tried to flip over in his fingers. 'North,' he said, and marked it red. By the evening, every magnet had a dot.
That night, Thatha found one magnet with a crack across it. It snapped into two half moons in his fingers. 'Now I have a north half and a south half,' he said.

Lakshmi held each half near the red dot. One face of each half was pushed away, and the other face was pulled in. 'No, Thatha,' she laughed. 'Each half has its own north and its own south. You cannot get a north pole on its own.'

On Saturday, the fifty trains went to Bengaluru. Every carriage could join every other carriage, front to back, in any order. Paati gave the last train to Lakshmi, with a red dot painted under the engine, for the girl who had noticed the twist.
story.epiphany: For the parent: every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. The green carriage was facing north to north, so it was repelled. It also twisted, because a magnet that is pushed away tends to turn round until it faces the other way and is attracted. Lakshmi found north by letting one magnet float and turn freely, as Petrus Peregrinus did in 1269. After that, she used repelling to sort the rest, because only a magnet can repel a magnet. The broken magnet showed that each piece of a magnet has both poles.
ask: Why did the green carriage slide away from the yellow one?
What small thing did Lakshmi notice that Thatha missed?
How did Lakshmi find out which face of the first magnet was north?
Why did pushing away tell Thatha more than sticking did?
When the magnet broke, Thatha expected a north half and a south half. What did Lakshmi find instead?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that magnets have a north and a south pole, and the rule for when they attract and repel? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: In August 1269, a French scholar called Petrus Peregrinus was in an army camp outside the town of Lucera, in southern Italy. While the army waited, he wrote a long letter about magnets to a friend. At that time, some people said a compass needle points north because there are great iron mines in the far north. Peregrinus said this could not be right. Magnet stones are found in many lands, yet needles everywhere point the same way. He also tested magnets himself. He put a lodestone, a natural magnet stone, in a wooden dish, and floated the dish in a big vessel of water. The stone turned until one end pointed north. He called that end its north pole. Then he brought a second lodestone close. A north pole drove the floating north pole away, but drew a south pole closer. In the end, he wrote, the north pole joins the south pole. He also broke a lodestone, and found that each piece had both poles. Peregrinus had a wrong idea too. He drew a wheel with iron teeth and a lodestone, and said it would turn forever, because the south pole would push the iron teeth away. But a magnet attracts iron with both poles. The wheel cannot work, and nobody has made one turn.
how_we_found_out.who: Petrus Peregrinus, also called Pierre de Maricourt, a French scholar of the 1200s.
how_we_found_out.when: His letter on the magnet is dated 8 August 1269.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People said compasses point north because of iron mines in the far north. Peregrinus showed this could not be right. He himself thought a magnet wheel could turn forever, because a south pole would repel iron. But iron is attracted by both poles, so such a wheel stops.
how_we_found_out.art: A medieval scholar in a tent in an army camp, watching a dark stone in a wooden dish float in a large tub of water, with a second stone in his hand.

experiments.title: Magnet Boats: what does a pushed-away magnet do?
experiments.context: In this experiment you float two bar magnets on plastic lids in a tub of water. You find their north poles, then test what happens when poles face each other, and what a pushed-away magnet does when you let it go.
experiments.question: When two floating magnets repel each other, do they stay apart?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Float two magnets with their north poles facing each other, and let go. Will they stay apart, drift away, or end up stuck together? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two magnets, the same lids and the same tub every time. Start each try with the magnets 10 cm apart, and let go gently without pushing. Only change which poles face each other. Do each pairing 3 times, because one try can be a fluke. Switch off the fan, because moving air pushes the lids.

materials.item: 2 bar magnets, about 5 to 8 cm long. School sets often mark the north end red or N.
2 plastic lids about as wide as your hand, such as tiffin or jam jar lids, or 2 small plastic plates
the widest plastic tub, basin or bucket you have, filled with water nearly to the top. Not steel.
a ruler
a strip of paper or tape and a pen, to label the poles
a phone with a compass app, or a compass, to check north

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips. Keep magnets away from phones, cards and small children's mouths.

schedule.what: Float one magnet to find its north pole. Label both magnets. Test north to south, north to north and south to south. Let the boats go and watch what they do.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for each try. Then draw what the two boats did after you let go, in three pictures.

flow.context: This is the first step of Magnet Boats. You float one magnet so it can turn freely, and find its north pole.
flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan. 2. Fill the tub with water nearly to the top. 3. Lay one magnet in the middle of a lid. 4. Float the lid in the middle of the tub. 5. Wait about a minute until it stops turning.
flow.say: A magnet that can turn freely settles pointing north and south. Let's see which end turns north.
flow.kid: Switch off the fan. Put a magnet on a lid. Float the lid in the middle. Wait. Watch it turn.
flow.parent: Keep the tub a metre from the fridge, the gas cylinder and steel almirahs, because iron nearby can turn the magnet. A full tub stops the lid from hitting the sides. The turning is slow. If the lid drifts to the edge, nudge it back with a pencil.

flow.do: 1. Check north with the phone compass, held at arm's length from the magnet. 2. Label the end pointing north 'N' and the other end 'S'. 3. Label the second magnet by holding its ends near the floating magnet's N end. The end that is pushed away is N.
flow.say: The end pointing north is the north pole. Now let's use it to find the north pole of the other magnet.
flow.kid: Which end points north? Write N on it. The other end is S. Now label the second magnet too.

ask.q: How can you tell which end of the second magnet is north?
good: The end that pushes the floating N end away is north.

flow.parent: A phone held right next to a magnet gives a wrong reading, so keep it an arm's length away. If your magnets are already marked, check that the marks are right.

flow.do: 1. Let the floating magnet settle. 2. Lay the ruler across the rim of the tub. 3. Hold the second magnet's S end 15 cm from the floating N end. 4. Move it closer slowly, about 1 cm every 2 seconds. 5. Stop when the boat first moves, and read the gap. 6. Do it 3 times, then repeat with N facing N.
flow.say: Let's find out how close a magnet must come before the boat feels its force. First south to north, then north to north.
flow.kid: Hold the S end far away. Move it closer, very slowly. Stop when the boat moves. Read the gap on the ruler. Write it down.
flow.parent: Water lets the boat move with very little force, so it often moves at 5 to 10 cm with school bar magnets. Your numbers will be different. With N facing N, the boat often turns as well as moving away. Write down what you see.

flow.do: Before the next test, ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Now we float both magnets, north facing north, 10 cm apart, and let go. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Both magnets will float, north facing north. What will happen when you let go? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the boats will do, and why?
good: Push apart, because like poles repel.
Any guess with a reason is good. The test will tell us.

flow.do: 1. Put the second magnet on the other lid. 2. Hold both lids still, 10 cm apart, north ends facing. 3. Let go gently at the same time. 4. Watch for 1 minute. 5. Do it 3 times, then 3 times with S facing S.
flow.say: Let go gently, without pushing. Just watch. What does each boat do first? And then?
flow.kid: Hold both boats. North faces north. Let go gently. Watch for one minute. What happens first? What happens next?

check.q: Two magnet boats start with their north poles facing. What usually happens after you let go?
options: They push apart, one turns round, and they stick together
check.why: Like poles repel, so at first the boats push apart. But the push also twists each magnet. A magnet that is free to turn swings round until a south pole faces the other north pole, and then they attract. Picking 'stay apart for ever' is what most people guess, because they think of repelling as the end of the story.

flow.parent: The lids usually push apart, turn, and then drift back together and bump. Sometimes they end up side by side, pointing opposite ways. That is also north facing south. If the boats drift apart and stop, gently nudge one a little closer.

flow.do: 1. Look at the table together. 2. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason. 3. Then explain the rule.
flow.say: What did the boats do every time? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why did the boats end up together, even when they started north facing north?
good: The magnet turned round until south faced north, and unlike poles attract.
Repelling pushes and twists the magnet, so it turns.

flow.think: Repelling only lasted while you held the boats straight. What does that tell you about magnets that are free to turn?

experiments.title: The Bumpy Slide: how many poles does a fridge magnet have?
experiments.context: In this experiment you slide two bendy fridge magnets over each other and feel for bumps. The bumps tell you how many poles are hidden on the magnet's face.
experiments.question: Does a bendy fridge magnet have just one north pole and one south pole, like a bar magnet?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Press two bendy fridge magnets face to face and slide one along. Will it slide smoothly, or will you feel bumps? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Slide the same two magnets across the same distance, 5 cm, at the same slow speed. Only change the direction: along the length, then across the width. Count the bumps 3 times each way.

materials.item: 2 bendy flat fridge magnets, the kind that come with shop or pizza adverts. Thin and flexible, not the hard round ones.
a ruler
a pair of scissors (a grown-up cuts)
a steel paper clip

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with the scissors.

schedule.what: Slide two fridge magnets face to face in two directions. Count the bumps in 5 cm. Cut a strip and test it.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the back of a fridge magnet with the stripes you think are there.

setup.art: Two bendy fridge magnets pressed together, magnetic side to magnetic side on a table, a child's finger sliding the top one.
setup.caption: 1. Put the magnets face to face. Slide one slowly.

setup.art: The same two magnets with the top one turned a quarter turn, and a ruler beside them marking 5 cm.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the top one a quarter turn. Slide again and count the bumps.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands cutting a thin strip off a fridge magnet with scissors, and the strip stuck to the fridge.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up cuts a strip. Does it still stick?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Bumpy Slide. You test whether a bendy fridge magnet acts like a bar magnet.
flow.do: 1. Put one magnet magnetic side up on the table. 2. Lay the other on top, magnetic side down.
flow.say: The magnetic side of each magnet is the side that holds to the fridge. Let's put the two magnetic sides together.
flow.kid: Put one magnet flat, magnetic side up. Lay the other on top, magnetic side down.
flow.parent: The magnetic side is the plain brown or black side, without the picture. If the two will not stay together, one is upside down.

flow.do: 1. Slide the top magnet slowly along its length for 5 cm, then across its width for 5 cm. 2. Count the bumps you feel each way. 3. Do each direction 3 times.
flow.say: Slide slowly and feel with your fingers. Does it slide smoothly, or does it bump? Count every bump.
flow.kid: Slide the top magnet slowly. Feel it. Count the bumps. Now turn it and slide the other way.
flow.parent: In one direction it usually slides smoothly, and in the other it bumps, often 10 to 20 times in 5 cm. If you feel bumps both ways, turn the top magnet a little until one way is smooth.

flow.do: 1. Try the back faces together. 2. Try the paper clip on the back face, then on the magnetic face.
flow.say: Does the back of the magnet attract anything?
flow.kid: Try the back sides together. Try the paper clip on the back. Then on the magnetic side.

check.q: When you slide two fridge magnets face to face one way, you feel many bumps. What does each bump show?
options: The magnet crossing from a stripe that attracts to one that repels
check.why: The magnetic face has thin stripes of north and south poles side by side. Sliding across the stripes, a north stripe meets a south stripe and attracts, then meets a north stripe and repels. That is the bump. Picking 'a crack' or 'dust' means looking for a fault, but the bumps are regular, so they come from a pattern.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a thin strip, about 1 cm wide, off one magnet. 2. Test the strip on the fridge. 3. Ask for a claim, the evidence and a reason.
flow.say: If we cut a strip off, will it still be a magnet? Let's see. Then tell me what you found and why.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up cut a strip. Does it stick to the fridge? What did you find out?

ask.q: How many poles do you think the fridge magnet has?
good: Many: one for each bump, in stripes.
More than two, because it bumped many times.

flow.think: A bar magnet has 2 poles. This flat magnet has many. Why might many poles hold better to a fridge?

activities.title: The Push You Can Feel
activities.context: This short activity is the way into the unit. You feel two magnets attract and repel with your own hands.

materials.item: 2 bar magnets
a smooth table

activities.safety: Do not let strong magnets snap onto fingers. Keep them away from phones.

schedule.what: Feel two magnets attract and repel. Chase one magnet across the table with the other, without touching.

activities.record: Draw two magnets that attract and two that repel. Use arrows.

setup.art: Two hands holding two bar magnets end to end with a small gap.
setup.caption: 1. Bring the ends slowly together.

setup.art: One bar magnet on a table sliding away from another that is pushed towards it, never touching.
setup.caption: 2. Chase one magnet across the table without touching it.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Push You Can Feel. You notice that magnets do two different things.
flow.do: 1. Give your child a magnet in each hand. 2. Ask them to bring the ends slowly together. 3. Then turn one magnet round and try again.
flow.say: Bring the ends together slowly. What do you feel? Now turn one round. What changes?
flow.kid: Hold a magnet in each hand. Bring them slowly together. What do you feel? Turn one round. Try again.

ask.q: What did you feel the two times?
good: One way they pulled together, the other way they pushed apart.
A push I could feel, with nothing touching.

flow.do: 1. Lay one magnet on the table. 2. Push the other magnet towards it, end to end, without touching. 3. Try to chase it to the edge of the table.
flow.say: Can you move the magnet on the table without touching it? Which way round must you hold yours?
flow.kid: Lay one magnet down. Can you chase it with the other one? No touching!
flow.parent: The magnet on the table often spins round and jumps onto the one in your child's hand. That is fine. It is exactly what the floating boats experiment looks at.

flow.do: Name the words: attract, repel, pole.
flow.say: When magnets pull together, we say they attract. When they push apart, we say they repel. The ends, where the force is strongest, are called poles.
flow.kid: Pulling together is called attract. Pushing apart is called repel. The ends are called poles.
flow.think: The magnet you chased often turned round. Why might it do that?

activities.title: Magnet or Plain Iron? The Wrapped Mystery
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up wraps a magnet and a plain piece of steel in paper so they look the same. You find out which is the magnet using only your own magnet.

materials.item: 2 bar magnets
a steel bolt, a big iron nail, or a steel spoon handle about as long as a magnet
2 sheets of newspaper and some tape

activities.safety: A grown-up wraps the nail so its point is covered.

schedule.what: Find out which wrapped object is a magnet by testing for attract and repel.

activities.record: Write what each end of each parcel did with your N end and your S end.

setup.art: Two paper parcels of the same size on a table, one hiding a bar magnet and one hiding a steel bolt.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up wraps a magnet and a steel bolt so they look the same.

setup.art: A child holding a labelled bar magnet's N end near one end of a parcel, which slides away.
setup.caption: 2. Test each end of each parcel with your N end and your S end.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Wrapped Mystery. A grown-up hides a magnet and a piece of steel in paper.
flow.do: Out of sight, wrap one magnet and the steel bolt in newspaper, so both parcels look the same. Mark them A and B.
flow.say: One of these parcels is a magnet. The other is plain steel. Can you find the magnet using only your magnet?
flow.kid: One parcel hides a magnet. One hides plain steel. Can you find the magnet?

flow.do: 1. Let your child test both ends of each parcel with the N end, then the S end, of their magnet. 2. Ask them to write what happens.
flow.say: Try both ends of each parcel with your north pole, then your south pole. What happens each time?
flow.kid: Try your N end on each end of parcel A. Then your S end. Now parcel B. Write what happens.

check.q: Parcel A is attracted by your N end and by your S end. Parcel B is pushed away by your N end at one of its ends. Which parcel is the magnet?
options: Parcel A, because it was attracted both times
check.why: Plain steel is attracted by both poles, so attraction does not prove anything. Only a magnet can repel a magnet. So parcel B is the magnet. Picking parcel A is a very common mistake, because sticking looks like the best sign of a magnet.

flow.do: Unwrap the parcels and check.
flow.say: Why was the push the only test that could tell us?
flow.kid: Unwrap them. Were you right? Why was the push the best clue?

ask.q: Why can't sticking tell you which one is the magnet?
good: Plain steel sticks to both ends of a magnet too.

activities.title: Floating Rings on a Pencil
activities.context: In this activity you make ring magnets float one above another on a pencil. Then you see what the pencil was really doing. You need ring magnets with a hole in the middle. Some school magnet sets have them.

materials.item: 3 or 4 ring magnets with a hole wider than a pencil
a round pencil
a lump of clay or atta dough, to stand the pencil up

activities.safety: Ring magnets can snap together hard and pinch skin. Keep them away from small children.

schedule.what: Float ring magnets on a pencil. Then take the pencil away and see what the top ring does.

activities.record: Draw the floating rings, and label each face N or S.

setup.art: A pencil standing in a lump of atta dough with three ring magnets on it, each floating above the one below with a gap.
setup.caption: 1. Thread the rings so each one repels the one below.

setup.art: A hand lifting the top ring off the pencil and the ring flipping over in the air to stick to the ring below.
setup.caption: 2. Take the top ring off the pencil and hold it above the others. What does it do?

flow.context: This is the first step of Floating Rings. You make magnets float using repelling.
flow.do: 1. Stand the pencil in the dough. 2. Drop a ring on. 3. Drop the next ring on. If it sticks, take it off, flip it over, and drop it on again.
flow.say: If the rings face like poles, they will repel. Let's make each ring float above the one below.
flow.kid: Stand the pencil up. Drop on a ring. Drop on the next. Does it stick? Flip it over!

flow.do: 1. Press the top ring down and let go. 2. Then lift the top ring off the pencil and hold it above the others with your fingers.
flow.say: Press the top ring down. What happens? Now lift it off and try to hold it floating without the pencil.
flow.kid: Press the top ring and let go. Now lift it off. Can it float without the pencil?
flow.parent: Without the pencil, the ring tips over and flips to stick, or slides off to one side. The pencil was stopping it from turning.

flow.do: Talk about what the pencil does.
flow.say: The magnets did the pushing. What did the pencil do?
flow.kid: The magnets push. What job does the pencil do?

ask.q: Why did the ring flip over without the pencil?
good: It turned round until it could attract.

activities.title: Draw the Magnet Inside
activities.context: In this drawing activity you draw what you think is inside a magnet, and what happens when it is cut in two.

materials.item: paper, a pencil, and red and blue crayons

schedule.what: Draw a bar magnet full of tiny arrow magnets. Then draw it cut in two and label the new poles.

activities.record: Keep the drawing in your science notebook.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a long bar magnet filled with small arrows all pointing the same way.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a bar magnet full of tiny arrow magnets, all pointing one way.

setup.art: The same drawing cut in two with a dotted line, and new N and S labels on each side of the cut.
setup.caption: 2. Draw it cut in two. Label the poles on each piece.

flow.context: This is the first step of Draw the Magnet Inside. You draw a model of what a magnet is made of.
flow.do: 1. Draw a long rectangle. 2. Fill it with 20 small arrows, all pointing to the right. 3. Colour each arrow's head red and its tail blue.
flow.say: Each arrow is a tiny magnet. The red head is its north, the blue tail is its south. Where do all the red heads come out?
flow.kid: Draw a long box. Fill it with little arrows, all pointing right. Colour the heads red and the tails blue.

flow.do: 1. Draw a line across the middle of the magnet. 2. Draw the two halves apart. 3. Label N and S on each half.
flow.say: Now cut the magnet in your drawing. Look at the arrows next to the cut. What poles do they make?
flow.kid: Draw a cut across the middle. Draw the two halves apart. Write N and S on each half.

check.q: A bar magnet is cut in half across the middle. What do you get?
options: A north half and a south half
Two magnets, each with a north and a south pole
Two pieces that are not magnets
check.why: The tiny magnets inside still point the same way in each half. So each half has north heads coming out at one end and south tails at the other. Picking 'a north half and a south half' is the most common guess, because the poles seem to belong to the ends.

flow.do: Ask what would happen if you kept cutting.
flow.say: What if we cut each half again, and again?
flow.kid: What if you cut it again and again? Draw the smallest piece.
flow.think: Is there a piece so small that it has only a north pole?

games.title: North and South Tag
games.context: This is a moving game for two or more players, slow enough for a room in a flat. Every player is a magnet with a north and a south pole, and must follow the rule: unlike poles attract, like poles repel.

printables.title: Pole badges: print, cut out and tape on
items: N badge for the front of your T-shirt
S badge for the back of your T-shirt
N badge for the back (swap card)
S badge for the front (swap card)

rules: Each player tapes an N badge on their front and an S badge on their back.
Players walk slowly around the room. No running.
When the caller says 'Freeze', each player looks at the nearest player.
If your N faces their S, you attract: hold hands and walk together as one magnet.
If your N faces their N, or your S faces their S, you repel: step back three steps.
If the caller says 'Turn', every player turns round, so front and back swap.
The game ends when everyone is in one long chain, front to back.

flow.context: This is the first step of North and South Tag, a moving game where each player is a magnet.
flow.do: 1. Tape an N badge on each player's front and an S badge on their back. 2. Clear a space and push chairs aside.
flow.say: You are each a magnet. Your front is your north pole and your back is your south pole.
flow.kid: You are a magnet now. Your front is north. Your back is south.

flow.do: 1. Everyone walks slowly. 2. Call 'Freeze' every 20 seconds. 3. Players check the nearest player and attract or repel. 4. Sometimes call 'Turn'.
flow.say: Freeze! Look at your nearest magnet. Do your poles attract or repel?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. On 'Freeze', look at the nearest player. Does your front face their back? Hold hands! Front to front? Step back!
flow.parent: Two people front to front have north facing north, so they repel. Front to back joins them into a longer magnet, still with N at the front and S at the back.

flow.do: When everyone is in one chain, ask a question.
flow.say: Our whole chain is now one long magnet. Where is its north pole? Where is its south pole?
flow.kid: You are one long magnet now. Where is its north? Where is its south?

check.q: Five players join front to back. The chain has a north pole at the front. What is at the very back?
check.why: Like a row of magnets joined north to south, the chain has one north pole at one end and one south pole at the other. Picking 'another north pole' means thinking a magnet could have the same pole at both ends. No magnet does.

setup.art: Two children with N badges on their fronts and S badges on their backs, walking slowly in a living room.
setup.caption: 1. Tape on your N and S badges.

setup.art: Three children joined in a chain, each holding the shoulders of the one in front, front to back.
setup.caption: 2. Front to back attracts. Front to front repels.

games.title: Pole Dominoes
games.context: This is a card game like dominoes. Each card is a magnet with a pole at each end. A card can only join another card where unlike poles meet.

printables.title: 28 magnet cards to cut out
items: 8 cards with N on the left and S on the right, drawn as red-and-blue bar magnets
8 cards with S on the left and N on the right
4 'Iron' cards: grey nails with no poles

rules: Shuffle the cards and give each player 5. Put the rest face down in a pile.
Lay one magnet card in the middle.
On your turn, add a magnet card at either end, where an N meets an S. If you have none that fits, take a card from the pile.
An Iron card can join any pole, because iron is attracted by both. The chain ends there on that side.
A Turn round card lets you turn one of your own cards round before you play it.
A Cut card lets you cut any card in your hand into two: draw a line across it, and each half gets an N and an S.
The first player with no cards left wins. Playing alone: lay out all the cards in as long a chain as you can.

flow.context: This is the first step of Pole Dominoes, a card game about joining magnets.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Shuffle and deal 5 to each player. 3. Lay one magnet card in the middle.
flow.say: Each card is a magnet. They join only where a north meets a south.
flow.kid: Each card is a magnet. You can join cards where N meets S.

flow.do: Take turns adding cards. Say the rule out loud each time.
flow.say: Which end can you join? Say why.
flow.kid: Add a card where N meets S. Say the rule out loud: unlike poles attract.
flow.parent: When a player uses a Cut card, ask them to label both halves. Each half must get an N and an S.

flow.do: End with a question.
flow.say: The Iron card joins any pole, but nothing can join after it. Why?
flow.kid: Why does the Iron card join any pole?

check.q: Why can the Iron card join a north pole or a south pole?
options: Iron is attracted by both poles
check.why: Plain iron becomes a temporary magnet with the opposite pole facing whichever pole is near, so it is always attracted. Picking 'Iron is a north pole' mixes up plain iron with a magnet.

setup.art: Printed cards showing small red-and-blue bar magnets, with N and S on their ends, spread on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and deal 5 each.

setup.art: A chain of magnet cards laid end to end on a table, every join an N meeting an S.
setup.caption: 2. Join cards only where N meets S.

projects.title: The Repel Racer
projects.context: In this two-day project you build a small car that you drive without touching it, by pushing it with a magnet's like pole.

materials.item: an empty matchbox or a small cardboard box
2 round pencils or 4 bottle caps for wheels, with 2 straws and 2 bamboo skewers for axles
2 bar magnets
tape and scissors
a long table or a smooth floor, and books to make the walls of a track

projects.safety: A grown-up pushes the skewers through the bottle caps. Skewer points are sharp.

schedule.what: Build the car and tape a magnet on top. Test it with the other magnet.
Build a track with books. Race the car along it by repelling, and time each try.

projects.record: Draw your car. Write the time for each race and what made the car turn or stop.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Repel Racer, a two-day project. You build a car you can drive with a magnet.
flow.do: 1. Push skewers through 2 straws for axles. 2. Fix a bottle cap on each end of each skewer. 3. Tape the straws under the matchbox. 4. Tape a bar magnet on top, N end at the back.
flow.say: If the back of the car is a north pole, what pole must your hand magnet have to push it?
flow.kid: Build the car. Tape the magnet on top, N at the back. Push it with your magnet. Which end pushes it?
flow.parent: The simplest car is a matchbox resting on two round pencils, which roll like logs. Bottle caps work better but need a grown-up to make holes.

flow.do: 1. Make a track 1 metre long with books for walls. 2. Push the car along by repelling, without touching. 3. Time three races.
flow.say: Drive it from one end to the other without touching. What happens if you come too close or too fast?
flow.kid: Drive the car down the track with your magnet. No touching! Time it. Try three times.
flow.wait: Come back tomorrow for the track and the races.
flow.parent: The car often swings round and jumps onto the hand magnet. The book walls help stop it turning. That is the same thing the floating boats did.

setup.art: A matchbox car with bottle-cap wheels and a bar magnet taped on top, N at the back.
setup.caption: 1. Build a small car and tape a magnet on top.

setup.art: A child pushing the car along a track of books with a hand-held magnet, a gap between the two magnets.
setup.caption: 2. Drive it along a track by repelling. No touching.

challenges.title: Make a Magnet Hover
challenges.context: In this challenge you try to make one magnet hover above another, with a gap and no touching. It is harder than it sounds.
challenges.problem: Make one magnet float in the air above another magnet, using only repelling. It must not touch the other magnet.
constraints: Use magnets and things from home.
The floating magnet must hover with a gap you can slide a sheet of paper through.
It must stay for at least 10 seconds.
materials: pencils, straws, a clear plastic bottle or glass
tape, thread, clay or atta dough
general: Put ring magnets on a pencil, so that like poles face each other. The pencil stops the top ring from turning.
Put bar magnets inside a clear plastic tube or tall glass that just fits them, so they cannot turn round.
Tie a thread to the floating magnet and tape the thread down, so it hovers but cannot flip.
creative: A toy called the Levitron floats a spinning top above a base magnet. The spin stops it flipping over, as a spinning top stays up.
Some trains, like the one to Shanghai airport in China, float on magnets that are controlled by electricity many times a second.
Scientists have floated a magnet above a superconductor, a very cold material that pushes back on magnetic fields.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to stop the floating magnet from turning. Draw it, build it, and time how long it hovers.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Hover challenge. First you see the problem.
flow.do: Hold one magnet flat on the table. Try to make the other hover above it, north over north, with your fingers off.
flow.say: Can you make it hover just by letting go? What does it do?
flow.kid: Try to make one magnet float above the other. Let go. What happens?
flow.parent: It flips over and sticks, or slides off sideways. This is the same thing the floating boats did.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: The magnet keeps turning or sliding. How could we stop that?
flow.kid: Draw three ideas to stop the magnet turning.

flow.do: Build your best idea and test it. Slide paper through the gap. Time it.
flow.say: Does it hover? Does paper fit through the gap? How long does it stay?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Does paper fit under it? Time it.
flow.parent: Help with cutting bottles. The pencil and ring magnets usually work best.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together.
flow.say: In every way that works, something stops the magnet turning. What did that in yours?
flow.kid: What stopped your magnet from turning?

check.q: Why does a hovering magnet always need something extra, like a pencil or a tube?
options: Magnets are too heavy to float
A free magnet turns round and then attracts
check.why: Repelling pushes the magnet, but it also twists it. Left free, it turns until unlike poles face and then it is attracted. Something must stop it turning. Picking 'too heavy' misses that repelling is easily strong enough to lift a magnet.

setup.art: A bar magnet flipping over in the air above another bar magnet on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Try it with no help. The top magnet flips.

setup.art: Ring magnets hovering on a pencil, with a sheet of paper slid into the gap.
setup.caption: 2. Find a way to stop it turning. Test with a sheet of paper.

items.p: Meenakshi brings the north pole of one magnet near the south pole of another. What happens?
items.why: Unlike poles attract. A north pole and a south pole are unlike poles. A strong answer says the rule, not just the answer.

items.p: Kavya pushes two south poles towards each other. What does she feel?
items.why: Two south poles are like poles, and like poles repel. So Kavya feels a push, even before the magnets touch.

items.p: Divya rolls a bar magnet in a pile of paper clips. Where do most clips cling?
items.why: A magnet's force is strongest at its poles. On a bar magnet, the poles are at the two ends. Picking 'the middle' usually means thinking the force is strongest where the magnet is thickest or heaviest.

items.p: Farhan floats a bar magnet on a plastic lid in a tub of water. It stops turning. What does its north pole point to?
items.why: A magnet that can turn freely settles pointing north and south. That is how the north pole got its name.

items.p: Anjali holds a steel spoon near the north pole of a magnet, then near the south pole. What happens?
opts: It is attracted to north and repelled by south
items.why: Plain steel is attracted by both poles. The spoon becomes a temporary magnet, with the opposite pole facing whichever pole is near it.

items.p: Lakshmi says, 'If two things stick together, both must be magnets.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A magnet sticks to a steel spoon, and the spoon is not a magnet. A strong answer says that only repelling proves that both are magnets.

items.p: True or false: a magnet always has both a north pole and a south pole.
items.why: True. Every magnet ever found has both poles. Cut it in two, and each piece still has both.

items.p: Two north poles push each other away. We say they ____ each other.
items.why: Repel means push away without touching. Like poles repel.

items.p: Match each pair of poles to what they do.
pairs: North pole and a plain iron nail
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Unlike poles attract and like poles repel. Plain iron is attracted by either pole.

items.p: Revathi tests things with the north pole of her magnet. Sort what each one can do.
items.a: see items
items.why: Plain iron and steel are attracted by both poles. Only a magnet can be repelled. A strong answer sorts by whether the thing is a magnet, not by how strong it is.

items.p: Put the steps in order for finding the north pole of an unmarked magnet.
items: Label the end that points north 'N'
Float the magnet on a plastic lid in a tub of water
Check which way is north with a compass
a: Float the magnet on a plastic lid in a tub of water
Check which way is north with a compass
Label the end that points north 'N'
items.why: The magnet must be free to turn and must stop before you can read it. Then you check north and label.

items.p: Remember the Magnet Boats, where two magnets floated on lids in a tub of water. What did the boats do when they started north facing north? Write what you saw.
items.a: They pushed apart, then one turned round, and then they came together and stuck.
items.why: A strong answer describes both parts: first the push apart, then the turning and attracting.

items.p: Why is repelling a better test for a magnet than sticking?
items.a: Plain iron and steel stick to a magnet too. Only a magnet can repel another magnet.
items.why: A strong answer says that attraction happens with plain iron as well, so only a push proves the thing is a magnet.

items.p: Draw two bar magnets that attract and two that repel. Label every pole N or S, and draw arrows to show which way each magnet is pushed or pulled.
items.a: Attracting pair: N facing S, arrows pointing towards each other. Repelling pair: N facing N or S facing S, arrows pointing apart.
items.why: A strong drawing labels all four poles and puts the arrows the right way round.
items.art: Two blank pairs of bar magnet outlines.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi each have an unmarked bar magnet. They argue about how to find the north pole.

views.says: Float it on water and see which end turns north.
Hold it near my magnet, which is marked. If its end pushes my N away, that end is north.

items.ask: Which way do you think is better? Give a reason. Then say one good thing about the other way.
items.a: Both ways work. Nandini's way needs no other magnet, only a tub of water, and it shows why the pole is called north. Shreya's way is quicker, but only works if her own magnet is marked correctly. A strong answer picks one with a reason and gives the other its due.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each way has a strength. Peregrinus used floating in 1269, then used one known magnet to test others.

items.p: Zoya cuts a bar magnet in half across the middle. What does she get?
opts: A north piece and a south piece
Two magnets, each with a north and a south pole
items.why: Each piece has a north pole and a south pole. New poles appear at the cut. Picking 'a north piece and a south piece' is the most common guess.

items.p: A compass needle's north pole points towards the Earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic. What kind of pole must that be?
items.why: Unlike poles attract. The needle's north pole is attracted there, so the Earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic is a south pole.

items.p: Priya's toy train carriages have magnets at each end. One carriage will not join the next. What should she try first?
items.why: If like poles are facing, the carriages repel. Turning one round makes unlike poles face, and they attract.

items.p: Ishita moves a magnet slowly towards a floating magnet boat. When does the boat start to move?
opts: As soon as the magnet is in the room
When the magnet comes within a few centimetres
items.why: Magnetic force gets weaker very quickly with distance. Far away it is too weak to move the boat. Within a few centimetres it is strong enough.

items.p: Two bendy fridge magnets slide smoothly one way but bump the other way. What does that tell you?
opts: Its face has stripes of north and south poles
items.why: Each bump is the magnet crossing a stripe that attracts and then one that repels. So the face has many poles in stripes.

items.p: Arjun says, 'The north pole of a bar magnet is stronger than the south pole.' Is he right?
items.why: False. Both poles of a bar magnet are equally strong. A strong answer suggests a test: count the paper clips each end can pick up.

items.p: A piece of steel that acts as a magnet only while a magnet is near it is called a ____ magnet.
items.why: A paper clip touching a magnet can hold another clip. Take the magnet away, and the second clip falls.

items.p: Three of these pairs repel. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: The north poles of two compass needles
items.why: North and south are unlike poles, so they attract. The other three are like poles, so they repel.

items.p: Put these in order, from what you see first to what you see last, when two magnet boats start north facing north.
items.why: First like poles repel, then the twist turns a magnet round, then unlike poles attract.

items.p: Label the poles on this drawing of three magnets joined in a row, end to end: write N or S at each of the six ends.
items.a: Each magnet has N at one end and S at the other, and at every join an N meets an S. For example: N S, N S, N S from left to right.
items.why: Magnets in a chain join only where unlike poles meet. A strong answer checks every join.
items.art: Three bar magnet outlines touching end to end, with six blank labels.

items.p: Remember the ring magnets floating on a pencil. Why did the top ring flip over when you took it off the pencil?
items.a: Without the pencil, the ring was free to turn. It turned until its other face pointed down, and then it was attracted.
items.why: A strong answer says the pencil stopped the turning, and a free magnet turns to attract.

items.p: Remember the Magnet Boats. Why did you start each try with the magnets 10 cm apart?
items.a: So every try was fair. If one try started closer, the force would be stronger, and the result would not be comparable.
items.why: A strong answer explains that changing the gap changes the force, so it must be the same each time.

items.p: In the story, Lakshmi's grandfather, Thatha, broke a round magnet into two halves. He thought he had a north half and a south half. Explain to him what is really true.
items.a: Each half has its own north and south pole. You can test it: one face of each half repels a north pole and the other face attracts it.
items.why: A strong answer gives the fact and a way to test it.

items.p: A compass needle is a small magnet. Why does a compass go wrong when you hold a magnet near it?
items.a: The magnet's poles are much closer than the Earth's poles, so they attract or repel the needle's poles more strongly.
items.why: A strong answer uses the rule of poles and says that nearby force is stronger.

items.p: In a science club in Hyderabad, two children argue about the Earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic.

views.says: It should be called the North Magnetic Pole. It is in the north, and everyone uses that name.
It should be called a south pole. It attracts the north poles of compasses, so it must be a south pole.

items.ask: Which name would you use? Give a reason. Then say what the other child has right.
items.a: Both have a point. Swathi is right that the name tells you where the place is, and changing it would confuse maps. Rohan is right about what kind of magnetic pole it is. A strong answer picks a side, gives a reason, and gives the other side its due.
items.why: Names can describe where something is or what it does. This name describes where.

items.p: Two magnet boats start south facing south, and you let go. Which picture shows how they end?
opts: Touching, north of one facing south of the other
items.why: Like poles repel and twist the magnets. A boat turns until unlike poles face, then the boats attract and touch.

items.p: A magnet is cut into 4 pieces. How many north poles are there now?
items.why: Each piece is a whole magnet with a north and a south pole. So 4 pieces give 4 north poles and 4 south poles.

items.p: Petrus Peregrinus drew a wheel with iron teeth and a magnet, and thought it would turn forever, because the south pole would push the iron away. What was wrong?
opts: Iron is attracted by both poles
Magnets do not work in Italy
items.why: A magnet attracts plain iron with both poles. So no pole pushed the teeth away, and the wheel could not keep turning.

items.p: On 14 February 1982, a detector at Stanford University recorded one signal that looked like a north pole on its own. Why do scientists still say nobody knows if such poles exist?
opts: The signal was never seen again
items.why: In science, one result that never happens again is not enough. Many bigger searches since have found nothing.

items.p: True or false: a magnet hanging on a thread can be repelled by another magnet and stay facing it, without turning, for as long as you like.
items.why: False. A magnet on a thread is free to turn. When repelled, it twists round until unlike poles face, and then it is attracted.

items.p: Sort what these magnet tricks need to work.
items: ring magnets floating on a pencil
a magnet sticking to a fridge
a car pushed by repelling along a track
two magnets joining north to south
items.a: see items
items.why: Attracting is what free magnets end up doing on their own. Repelling only lasts while something stops the magnet from turning: a pencil, book walls or your fingers.

items.p: Put these in the order they were found out.
items: Samuel Earnshaw proves that ordinary magnets alone cannot hold a magnet floating still
Petrus Peregrinus writes the rule that like poles repel
A detector at Stanford records one possible single pole
a: Petrus Peregrinus writes the rule that like poles repel
Samuel Earnshaw proves that ordinary magnets alone cannot hold a magnet floating still
A detector at Stanford records one possible single pole
items.why: Peregrinus wrote in 1269, Earnshaw in 1842, and the Stanford signal was in 1982.

items.p: Your friend Sneha says, 'Repelling and attracting are two different forces.' Use what the Magnet Boats did to answer her.
items.a: It is the same magnetic force. Which one you get depends only on which way the magnets face. The boats repelled, turned round, then attracted, with no change except the direction they faced.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence that turning a magnet changes repel into attract.

items.p: Design a test to find out whether a magnet's north pole and south pole are equally strong. Say what you would keep the same.
items.a: Count how many paper clips each pole can hold in a chain, using the same clips and the same magnet, 3 times each. Keep the clips, the magnet and the way you hang them the same.
items.why: A strong answer changes only which pole is tested, and repeats it.

items.p: A bendy fridge magnet has many poles in thin stripes. Why might that help it hold to the fridge but not attract things far away?
items.a: Neighbouring north and south stripes are close together, so their forces are strong right at the face. A little further away, the forces from the north and south stripes cancel out.
items.why: A strong answer says the stripes act strongly close up and cancel out further away.

items.p: A shop sells a 'north pole magnet' that it says has no south pole. What would you test to check the claim?
items.a: Hold it near the north pole of a marked magnet, then turn it round. If one side is repelled and the other attracted, it has both poles. Also float it to see if it points north and south.
items.why: A strong answer uses repelling and attracting to find both poles.

items.p: Why did the Repel Racer car often swing round and jump onto your hand magnet?
items.a: Repelling pushed the car but also twisted it. When it turned a little, its other pole faced my magnet and it was attracted.
items.why: A strong answer links the car to the free magnet in the boats experiment.

items.p: Draw three pictures of two floating magnet boats that start north facing north: at the start, halfway and at the end. Label the poles.
items.a: Start: N facing N with a gap. Halfway: one boat turning. End: N of one touching S of the other, or side by side pointing opposite ways.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the turning step and labels every pole.
items.art: Three empty boxes in a row.

items.p: Label the Earth drawing: the geographic North Pole, the magnetic pole in the Arctic, and what kind of magnetic pole it is (N or S).
items.a: The geographic North Pole at the top of the Earth's axis. The magnetic pole in the Arctic, a little away from it, marked S, because it attracts compass north poles.
items.why: A strong answer separates the place on the map from the kind of magnetic pole.
items.art: An outline of the Earth with an axis line and two blank labels near the top.

items.p: Three people talk about the magnet boats that always ended up stuck together.

views.says: Magnets prefer to attract. Repelling never lasts.
The boats turned because the push was not exactly in a straight line. With perfect aim, they could stay apart.
Even with perfect aim, the slightest wobble would turn them. So they always end up together.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Use what you saw in the experiment. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence from the boats, such as how often they turned. Meera is right that a perfectly straight push would not twist the magnet at first. Farhan is right that any tiny wobble grows, so in practice they turn. Kavya's 'prefer' is a way of saying what free magnets end up doing.
items.why: This is a real question about balance. A balance that any wobble upsets is called unstable, and repelling magnets are in that kind of balance.

quiz.p: What are the two ends of a bar magnet called?
quiz.why: The ends, where the force is strongest, are called poles: a north pole and a south pole.

quiz.p: Usha holds a north pole near another north pole. What happens?
quiz.why: Like poles repel. Picking 'attract' mixes up the rule.

quiz.p: Sundari holds a south pole near a north pole. What happens?
Gita's magnet is floating on a lid in water. When it stops, the end pointing north is called what?
quiz.why: The north pole is the end that points north when the magnet is free to turn.

quiz.p: Which one can push away the north pole of a magnet?
opts: The north pole of another magnet
quiz.why: Only a magnet can repel a magnet. A nail and a spoon are plain steel, which is attracted by both poles.

quiz.p: Anu has two wrapped parcels. One pushes her magnet away. What is inside it?
quiz.why: Repelling is the sure test of a magnet.

quiz.p: Two magnet boats start north facing north, and Bhavana lets go. What do they usually do in the end?
quiz.why: They push apart, but the push twists them. One turns until unlike poles face, then they attract.

quiz.p: In the Magnet Boats test, why do you let go gently, without pushing?
opts: So only the magnets move the boats
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. A push from your hand would mix up the result.

quiz.p: Selvi cuts a magnet in two. What does each piece have?
opts: A north and a south pole
quiz.why: Each piece is a whole magnet with both poles.

quiz.p: The Earth's magnetic pole in the Arctic attracts the north pole of a compass. What kind of pole is it?
quiz.why: Unlike poles attract, so it must be a magnetic south pole, even though it is in the north.

quiz.p: Why does a bendy fridge magnet bump when you slide it across another one?
opts: It has stripes of north and south poles
quiz.why: The face has thin stripes of poles. Crossing them you feel attract, repel, attract.

quiz.p: Who wrote the rule that like poles repel and unlike poles attract, in 1269?
quiz.why: Petrus Peregrinus wrote it in a letter from an army camp in Italy in 1269.

open_questions.q: Do magnetic monopoles, single north or south poles, exist anywhere?
open_questions.why_open: Some theories predict them. One possible signal was seen in 1982 and never again. Searches go on.

open_questions.q: Why do the Earth's magnetic poles sometimes swap places?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know it has happened many times from the rocks, and that the moving liquid iron in the core causes it, but cannot yet predict when it will happen next.

open_questions.q: What is an electron's magnetism, underneath?
open_questions.why_open: Every electron is a tiny magnet with two poles. Physicists can measure it very exactly, but nobody can say what it is made of, or whether that question even makes sense.

maths.problem: In the Magnet Boats test, Kavya found the boat moved at a gap of 6 cm, 5 cm and 7 cm in three tries, with north facing south. What is the middle value, and why use it?
maths.explain: Put the three numbers in order: 5, 6, 7. The middle one is 6 cm. Using the middle value stops one odd try from changing the answer too much.
maths.context: This is about the Magnet Boats test. You bring a magnet slowly towards a floating magnet and measure the gap when the boat first moves.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. Ordering the tries and taking the middle gives a fairer answer.

maths.problem: A bar magnet is cut into 2 pieces, then each piece is cut in 2 again, and then each of those in 2 again. How many north poles are there now?
maths.explain: After the first cut there are 2 magnets. After the second, 2 times 2 is 4. After the third, 4 times 2 is 8. Each piece has one north pole, so there are 8 north poles and 8 south poles.
maths.context: This is about cutting magnets. Each piece of a cut magnet is a whole magnet with a north and a south pole.
maths.why_maths: Doubling shows how quickly the number of poles grows, and that north and south poles always come in equal numbers.

maths.problem: Divya slid two fridge magnets 5 cm across each other and felt 15 bumps. About how wide is one stripe of poles, in millimetres? (5 cm is 50 mm.)
maths.explain: 50 mm shared among 15 bumps is a little over 3 mm each, because 15 times 3 is 45, close to 50. So the stripes of poles are about 3 mm apart.
maths.context: This is about the Bumpy Slide test, where you slide two bendy fridge magnets face to face and count the bumps.
maths.why_maths: We cannot see the stripes, but sharing the distance by the number of bumps tells us how wide they are.

maths.problem: In the Magnet Boats test, Farhan let the boats go north facing north 10 times. 9 times they turned and stuck together. Once they drifted apart and stopped. Draw a bar chart and say what it shows.
maths.answer: A bar of 9 for 'turned and stuck' and a bar of 1 for 'stayed apart'. Almost every time, a free magnet turned round and attracted.
maths.explain: The tall bar shows what usually happens. The one short bar is worth looking at: the boats may have drifted out of reach before they could turn.
maths.context: This is about the Magnet Boats test, where two magnets on floating lids start with their north poles facing and are let go.
